Land Grab Or Land Scam?

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
While tensions reach breaking point between residents and so called land invaders in Lenasia South, we expose a sophisticated criminal syndicate profiting from South Africa's unresolved land debate.

Unique Selling Point:
Last week friday, residents of Lenasia and surrounding areas staged yet another protest against what they termed a land invasion in the area. They blocked off roads surrounding several informal settlements that have sprung up in the Lenasia South area, where hundreds if not thousands of shacks have sprung up over the past few months next to suburban areas. Locals claimed that state owned land was being sold illegally, and that since the informal settlements have sprung up crime has increased in their neighbourhoods. But the so-called invaders have hit back at the residents, claiming the protests amount to nothing more than racism on the part of the Lenasia South residents. While tempers flare and allegations are hurled from both sides, our undercover footage reveals that a syndicate has taken advantage of the need for land in the area, and is selling state owned land to anyone with the money to pay for it, completely illegally.

Summary:
While the land debate continues in South Africa, and tempers flare between different races and classes and government has yet to address many of the inequalities of the past, unscrupulous syndicates are taking advantage of the situation and exploiting the real needs for their own financial gain, fuelling tensions across racial and class divides.

Further information:
We have footage of protests
We have hidden camera footage of "sales office" on one of the disputed areas of land in Len South, where land is sold for R1500 for a 15m x 20m stand. The syndicate also offers to build your shack for an extra cost.
We will interview both suburban residents as well as informal settlement residents to hear both sides of the story.
MMC Public Safety Michael Sun has agreed to give us a team from JMPD to accompany us into the "Lakeside" informal settlement where the "sales office and seller" from the hidden cam footage is located.
The mayor has agreed to an interview

Script:


Voice
Chaotic scenes in Lenasia South on the outskirts of Johannesburg two weeks ago, as rubber bullets flew and angry crowds clashed over alleged land invasions in the area. From Gauteng to the Western Cape, the hunger for land is driving people to violent extremes. Lenasia borders Soweto and Ennerdale – the southernmost part of the Municipality of Johannesburg. Tensions flared when fed up homeowners blocked off major roads surrounding informal settlements, like Lakeview and Narrin’s farm, which have sprung up on government owned land in recent months.

Link Devi
The conflict is a complex web of interests. On the one hand residents are concerned for their safety, and on the other side people who recently moved into the informal settlement believe they have a right to be here.

Voice
Maxwell Mudzwari recently bought a modest home in a new development in Lenasia South called Hillside. He says it took years of hard work to afford the home loan and escape to a better life.

Sound Up Maxwell
The main reason is that I wanted to move from the township. I wanted to start a new life. And my property specifically, it’s positioned in a way that if I walk out of my yard, when I look at this view, it completes my heart and my soul.

Voice
But his view is changing rapidly – across the road Lakeview has erupted from a few shacks last year to a sprawling development.

Sound Up Maxwell
Devi: An ordinary South African may say why did that bother you, because shacks are common place all over the country?

Maxwell: Crime. We are having a lot of issues here since we started having this.

Voice
Riaz Pather is a resident and community patroller from Lenasia South and says scenes like these, from housebreakings to violent armed robberies, have now become common.

Sound Up Riaz
Since we have these informal settlements, or squatter camps, mushrooming up all over the place, we’ve seen a drastic increase in crime.

Voice
The Lenasia South Residents Association, or LSRA, has been lobbying government to put a stop to what they call the ongoing land invasion. Ismail Sahib is the spokesperson.

Sound Up Ismail
Within the past 12 months, there’s been over 10 000 shacks erected in region G. 10 000 shacks equates to around roughly 40 000 people, that have come into an area where the infrastructure cannot handle so many people.

Voice
But the Residents’ Association believes this is no ordinary land grab – rather it’s government land being sold by opportunistic individuals.

Sound Up Ismail
We’re talking about a syndicate that’s enticing people to come in, and settle down. And obviously it’s opportunistic for them, because they are making money out of it.

Voice
It’s an allegation we heard repeatedly. Gugu Manana recently joined the protests for the same reason.

Sound Up Gugu
my view is that the people who are selling the stands, they are protecting their interests at our expense, and we find it very unfair.

Voice
Our investigators were told that a good place to start looking would be at Lakeview. We found a whole informal industry around the development, with people selling the poles and corrugated iron used to build the stands on site. We also found a few shacks like this one, marked office. So we decided to send undercover agents posing as a married couple to one of the “offices” with a hidden camera to ask if we could buy a plot of land.

Sound Up Hidden Camera
Investigator 1: How do we get land here?

Man: Can we talk inside? Ok, the ground is for free. You contribute R1500 for development in the place. We buy rolls of pipe, uprights, we put taps in, and up and there is sanitation running up and down.

Voice
While the salesman did not specifically offer to sell us the land, for R1500 we could have a stand of 15 by 20 m on the site, with access to water thrown into the deal.

Sound Up Hidden Camera
Man: You contribute R1500, come with your shack, we put you on the stand. Stands are 15m x 20m.

Voice
We were told a man named Farouk Jardin was in charge of the operation, so we asked him for an interview.

Sound Up Farouk
Devi: And what position, I mean you’re doing this interview as?

Farouk: The Ennerdale Stakeholders Association.

Voice
Jardin says the Association stepped in and took the City of Joburg to court in July last year after the city started forcibly evicting people from Lakeview.

Sound Up Farouk
We then made a plan, and we went to the high court for an urgent interdict. We were successful on the 20th of July last year. We got the urgent interdict.

Voice
Under the Prevention of Illegal Eviction from and Unlawful Occupation of Land, or PIE act, government may not randomly remove people from occupied land unless they can provide them with an alternative place to stay. The City and the Department of Human Development have since taken them to court again, but the cases were eventually dropped.

Sound Up Farouk
I’m saying, that land now belongs to us. Because they abandoned their right on that land when they abandoned their case.

Voice
Jardin denies that the money is to buy land – he says it’s for services and to pay for past and future legal fees.

Sound Up Farouk
Devi: So what’s the R1500 for?

Farouk: It covers those costs, the lawyers costs. Electricity was a private guy that was doing it. Water is, I mean I showed you the pipes earlier, and the fittings, that is what we are doing, we are providing the water.

Devi:
And who’s going to pay for the water?

Farouk: Well, right now, to be more precise, if you look at Ennerdale and other areas, lots of people are not paying for water. Council has a huge problem, because they can’t even get their billing right. So I mean that question, they can’t hold it against us.

Voice
But the LSRA say that the water supply in the area is under threat.

Sound Up Ismail
There’s constant water and electricity outages, so they would tap into the water line, and you’d find that the reservoir starts running down. This is not a monthly issue, this is a weekly issue.

Voice
Residents say the ongoing problems are hitting their pockets.

Sound Up Gugu
The bills are high, because the people are taking electricity from us. They are taking water from us. When people are gone to work, used to come and steal water, and make illegal connection of electricity while people don’t see. And then at the end of the month, your bill is too high.

Sound Up Maxwell
The overhead cables, it’s stolen. They cut the overhead cables, and they then start connecting electricity.

Voice
We found these illegal connections running from a city transformer, and followed the cables down the road to their destination.

Sound Up Devi
We’ve traced this cable for kilometers and it runs directly into Lakeview, no wonder there have been electricity supply problems in this area.

Voice
Jardin says they are getting the blame for problems that have been around for ages.

Sound Up Farouk
Farouk: I find it strange, because all these areas, all these years, they had neighbourhood watches.

Devi: Do you think you guys are getting blamed for general criminality?

Farouk: For everything. We’re blamed for foreigners, for everything.

Voice
The Residents Association believe there’s more to the land occupation than destitute people needing homes.

Sound up Ismail
we are talking about people that are looking at it from a money making point of view, that are renting out the shacks, and putting them up and selling it.

Sound Up Farouk
We cannot be naive, to say there aren’t people doing that behind our backs, you’ll find that.

Voice
But Jardin is adamant his motives are purely humanitarian.

Sound Up Farouk
Devi: Are you making a profit from the setup here?

Farouk: No, definitely not.

Voice
A short drive down the road from Lakeview is Narrin’s farm, mainly owned by government, with a small portion in private hands. Last friday we found JMPD breaking down some of the many NEW shacks here. For City of Joburg mayor Herman Mashaba it’s all about maintaining law and order.

Sound Up Herman Mashaba
If we continue in this way, in Johannesburg, in the City of Johannesburg, I can assure you this country will collapse eventually. Because there will be a total breakdown of the rule of law.

Voice
The shack demolitions have been met with strong opposition from land occupants. Jardin says they’re considering legal action against the city.

Sound Up Farouk
If you can put up a shack in a hour and a half, and take the next hour and a half to occupy it, and regard it as your home, nobody has a right to come and breakdown that shack. That is your right in terms of the constitution.

Voice
Gugu Manala says residents are not unsympathetic to the plight of the homeless, but ratepayers shouldn’t have to bear the brunt of government’s problems.

Sound Up Gugu
Where are you going to get the water, where are you going to get the electricity from? You’re getting it from me. Is it fair? No.

Voice
The mayor says the city simply does not get enough of a budget from national government to fulfil all its residents’ housing needs.

Sound Up Herman Mashaba
the amount of money that you get you can only build, if you’re lucky, two and a half, three thousand houses a year.

Voice
While government struggles to clear the housing backlog, the story of Lenasia South, of communities torn apart by anger and suspicion, seems set to continue.

Sound Up Ismail
Government is not just failing the destitute, but is failing the hardworking middle class as well, that’s trying to come up in life.
